title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Post-construction clean
audience: Owners of small post-construction cleaning businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting a builder, developer or property manager.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, and be clear when no local evidence exists.
Set a minimum charge for return visits and short jobs, and explain it to a builder before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on the state of the site when the crew arrives, the size and finish of the fit-out, the standard the builder specifies, the handover window, the equipment needed and the cost of running the business. A crew that can work across several handovers on one route protects its travel time. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly. The research found no post-construction hourly range. The office range from Clean Group ($35 to $65 per hour, updated 15 March 2026) is for office and business premises, not for handover work, so do not use it as a benchmark here. Build the rate from your own costs and hours.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel between sites, site induction, waiting for trades to clear an area, waiting for access, return visits for missed items, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. For example, if sixty of every hundred paid hours are billable, the costs of all one hundred hours must be recovered from the sixty, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, and its example gives 1,344 billable hours a year for 40 hours a week at 70 per cent (published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (page metadata dated 1 October 2026). Labour on-costs such as payroll tax, workers' compensation, training and unpaid travel can add 25 to 40 per cent on top of wages, and Jobber says cleaners often undercount them (31 March 2026). That is a US-leaning guide, and payroll tax and workers' compensation are set state by state, so use your own state's figures. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate. Xero's worked example shows the method: $93,000 to earn before tax, 46 working weeks and 25 billable hours in a 38-hour week give about $81 an hour (3 September 2026). That example is not a cleaning business. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for the owner before the rate is published. Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for return visits and short jobs
instruction.body: Return visits to fix missed items can cost more in time than they earn, because travel and set-up do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge covers the time needed to attend the site and start work. Cleaners either set a two- or three-hour minimum or a flat minimum. Jobber gives $100 as an example flat minimum and notes that a 30-minute job at $50 an hour leaves little profit after driving and overhead (31 March 2026). A contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin. Its figures are labelled illustrative, so use the method only: a $105 visit cost at a 30 per cent target margin gives a $150 minimum (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Agree in writing whether a return visit for your own missed item is charged at all, because the builder may expect it at no cost. State the minimum in writing before the visit.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, induction, admin, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate, and record that no local benchmark was found.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a return visit, and state the rule for missed items in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only. An owner needs $60,000 a year from billable work. The owner pays for 2,000 hours a year, but only 1,300 of them (65 per cent) can be billed to a builder. The owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What rate does each method produce, what does the business earn at the wrong rate, and what should be checked before the rate is published?
workedExamples.reasoning: Built from billable hours, the rate is $60,000 divided by 1,300, which is about $46.15 an hour. Built from all paid hours, the rate is $30 an hour, which looks lower. But only 1,300 hours can be sold, so $30 an hour brings in $39,000 and leaves a $21,000 gap. The rate must be built from billable hours. Then check it against the owner's own costs and the minimum charge for return visits, and confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation. No post-construction benchmark exists in the research to compare it with.

Price sheet with the base rate and the minimum charge

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking your costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, and record that no post-construction benchmark was found.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking return visits for missed items at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge and a rule for missed items that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC's pricing guidance (last modified 15 July 2026) says misleading statements about prices are prohibited. The research file does not confirm whether that guidance covers minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term, so check those points before publishing a price sheet. A contract term that lets one party alone change prices may be unfair, and the ACCC's small business guide (July 2021, an older source) warns of this. Check any rate-change clause in a handover contract.

Confirm the tax treatment of leave and superannuation for the owner with a registered tax agent before publishing the rate. Whether handover work is construction work, and which WHS and award rules then apply, is not settled by the research; check your state's rules. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and no unsourced benchmark is used.
A minimum charge and a missed-item rule are set and stated before any return visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge, the missed-item rule and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target. No post-construction benchmark was found, so keep your own record.
Set and state a minimum charge for return visits and short jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the builder pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for return visits?
options: Because return visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because builders expect every visit to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for handover work, given that the research found no post-construction benchmark?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, recorded and dated
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. Supports: billable time about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours. General range, not Australian.

Jobber, 'How Much to Charge for House Cleaning', https://getjobber.com/academy/cleaning/how-much-to-charge-for-house-cleaning/, dated 31 March 2026. Supports: labour on-costs of 25 to 40 per cent; two- or three-hour or flat minimums; $100 example flat minimum. US-leaning source.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: the rate built from take-home pay, business costs and super, divided by billable hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, dated 23 September 2026. Figures labelled illustrative; method only.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

ACCC, 'Small business and the Competition and Consumer Act', https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/Small%20business%20and%20the%20Competition%20and%20Consumer%20Act%20-%20July%202021.pdf, July 2021 (older source). Supports: a term that lets one party alone change prices may be unfair. Legal note, not pricing guidance.

Clean Group, 'Commercial cleaning pricing guide', https://www.clean-group.com.au/how-much-does-workplace-cleaning-cost-in-australia, updated 15 March 2026. Read to show that its $35 to $65 per hour range is for office premises and is not used here as a handover rate.
